n: The Passover is approaching — the yearly festival remembering Israel’s deliverance from Egypt, followed by a week of eating bread without yeast. Jerusalem swells with pilgrims.

f.g: A seven-day festival that began with the Passover meal.

n: The religious leaders are searching for a way to kill Jesus, but His popularity with the crowds makes them cautious.
Satan enters Judas Iscariot — one of the Twelve. Judas still chose to betray; Satan exploited a heart already open to him.

f.g: Possibly “man of Kerioth,” a town in Judea — perhaps the only apostle not from Galilee.

n: Judas goes to the chief priests and the temple police officers to discuss how to hand Jesus over.

f.g: Conferred, talked.
Officers of the temple guard, a Jewish police force.

n: The leaders are delighted and agree to pay him. Matthew records the amount: thirty pieces of silver.
Judas agrees and watches for an opportunity to betray Jesus away from the crowds.

f.w: in the absence of the multitude
f.g: Privately, when no crowd could protect Him.

n: The day arrives when Passover lambs are sacrificed at the temple. Jesus, the true Lamb of God, will soon be sacrificed too.

f.g: The Passover lambs were slaughtered on the afternoon of 14 Nisan.

n: Jesus sends Peter and John to prepare the Passover meal.

f.g: Preparing meant obtaining a lamb, unleavened bread, wine, and bitter herbs.

n: They ask where He wants it held. Jesus has kept the location secret, perhaps so Judas cannot betray Him before the meal.

f.g: Where do you want us to.

n: Their sign: a man carrying a water jar — unusual, since women typically carried water. Follow him to the house.

f.g: Men usually carried water in skins; a man with a jar would stand out.

n: They are to ask the homeowner, on the Teacher’s behalf, for the guest room where He will eat the Passover with His disciples.

f.g: Master or owner of the house.
Guest room.

n: He will show them a large, furnished upstairs room, ready with couches for reclining at the meal.

f.g: A room on a flat roof or second story; tradition later associated it with the gathering place in Acts.

n: Everything happens just as Jesus said, and they prepare the Passover.
When the time comes, Jesus reclines at the table with His apostles.

f.g: Literally “reclined,” the custom for the Passover meal as a sign of freedom.

n: Jesus tells them how deeply He has longed to share this Passover with them before He suffers. These are tender, intimate final hours.

f.g: A Hebrew way of expressing intense longing.

n: He will not eat it again until its meaning is fulfilled in God’s kingdom. Passover pointed to Him, and He is about to fulfill it.
He takes a cup — one of several in the Passover meal — gives thanks, and tells them to share it.

f.g: Greek eucharisteō, the root of “Eucharist.”

n: He won’t drink wine again until God’s kingdom comes. Latter-day revelation promises He will drink it again with His faithful Saints.

f.w: I will not drink of the fruit of the vine

n: Jesus takes bread, gives thanks, breaks it, and gives it to them: this is My body given for you; do this in remembrance of Me. He institutes the sacrament.

f.w: this do in remembrance of me

n: After the meal He takes the cup: this is the new covenant in My blood, shed for you. His death would seal a new covenant between God and His people.

f.g: The new covenant (testament and covenant translate the same Greek word).

n: Yet the betrayer is sharing this very table with Him. Sharing a meal made the betrayal even more painful.

f.w: the hand of him that betrayeth me

n: The Son of Man goes the way God has decreed, but that doesn’t excuse the betrayer. God’s foreknowledge never removes human responsibility.

f.g: A cry of grief as well as warning.

n: The apostles start asking one another who could do such a thing.

f.g: Question one another.

n: Shockingly, at this very meal, they begin arguing over who is the greatest.

f.g: A contentious dispute.

f.w: which of them should be accounted the greatest

n: Jesus contrasts His kingdom with worldly rulers, who dominate others while giving themselves flattering titles like “Benefactor.”

f.g: An honorary title rulers used for themselves (Greek Euergetēs).

n: Not so with His disciples. The greatest should be like the youngest, and the leader like a servant. Leadership in the Church is service.

f.g: The youngest in a household had the lowest status and did the menial tasks.

n: Who’s greater — the guest or the waiter? Normally the guest. But Jesus is among them as the one who serves. John records that this night He washed their feet.

f.w: I am among you as he that serveth

n: He thanks them for standing by Him through His trials.

f.g: Trials, testings.
Stayed loyal.

n: Just as the Father has given Him a kingdom, He gives them a kingdom.

f.w: I appoint unto you a kingdom
f.g: The word means to grant by covenant.

n: They will feast at His table and sit on thrones judging Israel’s twelve tribes. Latter-day revelation confirms the Twelve’s role in judging Israel.

f.w: judging the twelve tribes of Israel

n: Jesus speaks tenderly to Peter by his old name, repeating it: Satan has demanded to sift you all like wheat — shaking you violently to see what remains.

f.g: Shake in a sieve to separate grain from chaff; “you” here is plural — all the apostles.

n: But Jesus has prayed specifically for Peter that his faith won’t fail. When Peter has turned back, he must strengthen the others. Peter will lead the Church.

f.g: “Thee” here is singular — Jesus prayed for Peter personally.
When you have turned back.

n: Peter boldly insists he is ready to go to prison and even to die with Jesus.

f.w: both into prison, and to death

n: Jesus tells him that before the rooster crows that morning, Peter will deny knowing Him three times.

f.g: Roosters crow before dawn; “cockcrow” also named a watch of the night.

n: Jesus reminds them that when He sent them out with no money or supplies, they lacked nothing.

f.w: without purse, and scrip, and shoes

n: But now circumstances change: they’ll face hostility and need to provide for themselves. The talk of buying a sword is likely a vivid way of saying hard times are coming, not a call to arms.

f.g: Traveler’s bag.
Most interpreters see this as figurative; Jesus soon stops the use of a sword (v. 51).

n: Isaiah’s prophecy must be fulfilled: He will be counted among criminals. His life’s mission is reaching its end.

f.w: he was reckoned among the transgressors

n: Taking Him literally, they produce two swords. “That is enough,” He says — possibly meaning “Enough of this talk,” as they missed His point.

f.g: Perhaps “That’s enough!” — ending a conversation they had misunderstood.

n: Jesus goes out, as was His habit, to the Mount of Olives, and His disciples follow.

f.g: As He was accustomed.
Matthew and Mark name the place Gethsemane, “oil press.”

n: At the place, He urges them to pray that they won’t give in to temptation.

f.w: Pray that ye enter not into temptation

n: He moves about a stone’s throw away, kneels, and prays.

f.g: About as far as one could throw a stone.
Jews usually prayed standing; kneeling shows the intensity of this moment.

n: Father, if You are willing, take this cup from Me — yet not My will, but Yours. In this submission lies the heart of the Atonement.

f.g: A biblical symbol of suffering and divine judgment.

f.w: not my will, but thine, be done

n: An angel appears from heaven to strengthen Him. Only Luke records this. Heaven sustained Him but did not remove the burden.

f.w: an angel unto him from heaven
f.g: Verses 43–44 are missing from some early manuscripts but present in many others.

n: In anguish He prays even more intensely, and His sweat falls like great drops of blood. Latter-day scripture confirms that He bled from every pore as He took upon Himself the sins and suffering of all.

f.g: Greek agōnia, intense struggle like that of an athlete or warrior.

n: Rising from prayer, He finds the disciples asleep — exhausted by grief. Luke kindly explains that sorrow had worn them out.

f.g: Only Luke gives this sympathetic reason.

n: He asks why they sleep and urges them again to get up and pray so they won’t fall into temptation.
While He is still speaking, a crowd arrives, led by Judas, who approaches to kiss Jesus — the pre-arranged signal.

f.g: A kiss was a normal greeting of a disciple to his teacher — making the betrayal all the more bitter.

n: Jesus asks: Judas, are you betraying the Son of Man with a kiss? Even now, He addresses him by name, perhaps giving him a final chance.

f.w: betrayest thou the Son of man with a kiss?

n: Seeing what is about to happen, the disciples ask whether they should fight.

f.g: Strike.

n: One of them — John identifies him as Peter — strikes the high priest’s servant and cuts off his right ear.

f.w: the servant of the high priest
f.g: John names him Malchus.

n: Jesus says, “No more of this!” and touches the man’s ear, healing him — His last miracle of healing before the cross, performed for an enemy. Only Luke, the physician, records it.

f.g: “Let it be — no more of this.”

n: Jesus asks the leaders why they’ve come with swords and clubs as if He were a violent criminal.

f.g: Clubs.
A bandit or insurrectionist.

n: They never arrested Him in the temple during the day. But now it is their hour — the time when darkness has power.
They take Him to the high priest Caiaphas’s house. Peter follows at a distance.

f.g: The high priest was Caiaphas; his father-in-law Annas also questioned Jesus.

n: In the courtyard, people build a fire against the night chill. Peter sits down among them.

f.g: The open central courtyard of a large house.

n: A servant girl stares at him in the firelight and says he was with Jesus.

f.g: A servant girl.

n: Peter denies it: “Woman, I don’t know Him.” The first denial.
A little later someone else says he is one of them. “Man, I am not,” Peter replies. The second denial.

f.g: You are one of His disciples too.

n: About an hour later another person insists: he’s certainly one of them — he’s a Galilean. His accent gave him away.

f.g: Galileans had a distinctive regional accent.

n: Peter says he doesn’t know what they’re talking about. While the words are still in his mouth, the rooster crows. The third denial.
Only Luke records this heartbreaking moment: the Lord turns and looks at Peter. Peter remembers Jesus’ words. That look surely held sorrow — and love.

f.w: the Lord turned, and looked upon Peter
f.g: Jesus was apparently within sight across the courtyard.

n: Peter goes outside and weeps bitterly. His tears mark the beginning of his repentance; he will later become a mighty witness.
The guards holding Jesus mock Him and beat Him.

f.g: Struck Him.

n: They blindfold Him, strike His face, and taunt Him to prophesy who hit Him — mocking Him as a prophet while fulfilling His own prophecies.
They hurl many more insults at Him. Luke calls it blasphemy — they are mocking God Himself.

f.g: With irreverent insults against God.

n: At daybreak the council — elders, chief priests, and scribes — gathers and brings Him before them for a formal hearing.

f.g: The Sanhedrin, the 71-member Jewish high court.

n: They demand that He tell them plainly whether He is the Messiah. He replies that if He tells them, they won’t believe.
And if He asks them questions, they won’t answer or release Him. Their minds are made up.

f.g: The verdict was already decided.

n: From now on, He declares, the Son of Man will be seated at God’s right hand. He claims the position of divine power from Daniel and the Psalms.

f.w: sit on the right hand of the power of God

n: So they ask: are You the Son of God? He answers, “You say that I am” — a Hebrew way of saying yes, it is as you say.

f.g: An affirmative idiom: “You are right in saying I am.”

n: They need no other witnesses — they’ve heard it from His own mouth. They treat His testimony of truth as blasphemy worthy of death.

f.w: What need we any further witness?
